b: Asmodee is preparing to ramp up investment in its own publishing operations, major franchises and online platform Board Game Arena after posting record second-quarter revenues of €551.8m, as it looks to capitalise on the current boom in TCGs and renewed growth across its board game business.

The board game giant’s Q2 revenue was up almost 37% year-on-year – with its distribution of trading card games once again underpinning growth at the business, surging more than 51% year-on-year to €343.8m.
Asmodee’s board game revenue across publishing and distribution, meanwhile, climbed 18.4% to €167.5m, building on 16% growth in the preceding quarter.

More than 40% of that increase came thanks to Asmodee’s acquisition of French social and party game publisher ATM Gaming in April, in a deal which could reach €250m depending on ATM’s future performance.

Asmodee CFO Andrea Gasparini said in an earnings presentation that the remaining rise in board game revenue was split roughly equally between games published by Asmodee’s own studios and third-party titles it distributes for other publishers, with evergreen titles, expansions and new releases all contributing.
The company’s US revenue also recovered significantly in Q2, climbing 27.2% year-on-year to €70.1m after several difficult quarters impacted by US tariff volatility and wider economic uncertainty.

Asmodee had reported a 23% revenue slump from its US operations during the last three months of 2025 amid retailers reducing orders and adjusting inventories, followed by a 15% decline between January and March and another 9.4% fall between April and June this year.

Company CEO Thomas Koegler told the shareholder presentation the overall US tabletop market was now at an all-time high thanks to the TCG boom, while board games had also recovered from last year’s downturn.

He said, “We had a dip in the market last year mainly due to the tariffs,” adding that sales had recovered to levels seen a few years ago in some categories – although he said family games remained below their Covid-era highs.
He highlighted particularly strong demand for social and hobby games, describing the US market as being in “a good state”.

Asmodee’s own publishing operations have also returned to growth, with sales of games from its own studios rising 26.5% to €144.6m in Q2. That follows a 5.8% decline in the 2025/26 financial year, which Asmodee attributed to weaker Star Wars: Unlimited sales compared with the game’s strong post-launch period.

Koegler said about a third of the revenue increase from its own published titles came from the timing of Star Wars: Unlimited releases, another third from ATM Gaming and the remainder from other products.
Star Wars: Unlimited, published by Asmodee studio Fantasy Flight Games

ATM has also benefited from expanding its social games portfolio into more countries through its new owner’s distribution network, with the company reporting a 57% increase in sell-out volumes during the quarter – including strong demand for titles including Pili Pili and Mouton Mouton.

Asmodee’s improving publishing performance and soaring TCG revenues have left it with greater scope to invest in its business, with its adjusted EBITDA margin – a measure of its underlying profitability relative to revenue – reaching 18.1% for the last 12 months, exceeding its medium-term target for the first time.
Koegler said Asmodee would continue aiming to keep that figure above 18% while reinvesting in longer-term growth, although he expected profitability to improve more slowly than in recent quarters.
Gasparini said, “Priority number one is our portfolio of published products, because we want to bring them to the next level and create strong brands known as much as possible worldwide.”

He added that Asmodee would continue hiring key talent, strengthening its operations and investing in security and IT infrastructure, including AI tools and new systems for its front and back-office functions.

Gasparini also singled out Board Game Arena as one of Asmodee’s key strategic assets, saying the company believed there was further potential to strengthen the platform, expand its audience and diversify its games catalogue.

Koegler said the investment programme would include continued game development across Asmodee’s 23 studios, alongside efforts to increase international awareness of its established franchises, particularly Catan, Ticket to Ride, Dobble and Exploding Kittens.
He also highlighted the company’s efforts to establish the Asmodee name itself as a consumer-facing mark of quality, including a shop-in-shop operation at Fnac Les Ternes in Paris.

The publishing investment drive follows Asmodee’s appointment of former Exploding Kittens CEO Carly McGinnis as chief product officer in August, with responsibility for strengthening its publishing capabilities and bringing its studios and distribution teams closer together.

Asmodee’s financial firepower continues to be driven heavily by TCG distribution, however, with games published by third-party partners generating €395.6m during the quarter, up 42.4% year-on-year and accounting for almost 72% of total group revenue.

Pokémon’s 30th-anniversary products were a major contributor to the latest growth, alongside Magic: The Gathering and Riftbound, but Koegler said TCG demand was so strong that manufacturers were struggling to produce sufficient stock.

He said, “The entire industry is constrained on supply. Today, we sell what we have. We even allocate products to the best of what we can. One could say that the market is, for now, slightly underserved. It is just that the manufacturing capabilities of the suppliers are the limiting factor.”
He also said specialist hobby stores were experiencing significant growth, particularly those investing in organised play, demonstrations and other activities to engage their customers.
“Hobby stores are the heart of our industry,” he said, highlighting the positive impact of the trading card boom on both specialist shops and mass-market retailers.

Koegler nevertheless acknowledged that the growing number of TCGs was creating some competition for consumers’ spending, as well as difficulties for retailers trying to allocate cash, shelf space and attention between different games.
He said Asmodee was working with its publishing partners to spread TCG releases across the calendar where possible, helping retailers manage those competing demands.
Koegler added that the company’s pipeline of potential acquisitions remained as active as when it reignited its M&A strategy almost exactly two years ago, despite a string of deals since.

They include the big-money ATM buyout, as well as the acquisitions of Zombicide, Cthulhu: Death May Die, Sheriff of Nottingham and Japanese publisher Japon Brand from financially troubled CMON, and the rights to Time’s Up and Welcome To.
Asmodee also spent almost $175m in May to acquire the remaining 45% of Exploding Kittens it did not already own, five years after buying its initial majority stake.
Koegler added, “I think that expectations on valuations have become a bit more reasonable than in comparison to a few years back. We look confidently in our ability to pursue further acquisitions.”

Asmodee enters the crucial Christmas trading period confident of continued growth across both its own publishing operations and third-party distribution business, although Koegler cautioned that the pace might not match the latest quarter.
